english: I'm here to look at a place
usage: I came to look at a place
Polite; what you say walking into a 부동산 (real estate office)
I'm here to see a place
반말, only with a friend tagging along, not to the agent
I've come to look at places
Formal 합쇼체, a touch stiffer/more businesslike
I came to look at a room
Swap 방 ('room') when you want a one-room/studio (원룸)
examples: 안녕하세요, 집 보러 왔는데요.
Hi, I'm here to look at a place.
The standard opener the moment you step into the office
원룸 보러 왔는데요, 지금 볼 수 있는 거 있어요?
I came to see a studio — anything I can view now?
원룸 names the type; 볼 수 있는 거 asks what's viewable today
저 학교 근처에 집 보러 왔는데요, 예산은 한 오백에 오십이요.
I'm here to find a place near the school; my budget's about 5 million deposit, 500k a month.
한 ('about') + 오백/오십 states 보증금/월세 casually in 만원 units
nuance: 집 보러 왔는데요 is 집 ('house/home') + 보러 (the -러 'in order to' form of 보다 'to see') + 왔- (past of 오다 'come') + -는데요, the soft ender that opens a topic and waits for the agent to respond. So literally 'I came in order to see places, and…' — the universal first line when you walk into a 부동산. Here 보다 does NOT mean 'watch'; for housing it specifically means 'view/inspect a property', the way English says 'look at a place'. The dividing line from 집 구하러 왔는데요 ('I came to find/secure a place') is stage: 보러 is for the act of viewing today, while 구하러 frames the whole search for housing — both are natural, but 보러 is what you say when you're ready to actually walk through rooms. The English-speaker trap is dropping -는데요 and saying a flat 집 보러 왔어요, which is fine but blunter; the -는데요 invites the agent to take over ('what's your budget? this way…'). Another trap is using 찾다 ('to look for/search') as 집 찾으러 왔어요 — understandable, but for the agent-office context Koreans say 보러 (to view) or 구하러 (to secure), not 찾으러. Default to 존댓말 with any agent; 반말 here would be jarringly rude to a stranger doing business.

It's correct but abrupt as an opener. The soft ender 집 보러 왔는데요 hands the conversation to the agent and sounds like a real customer easing in.
Using 찾으러 instead of 보러/구하러.
찾다 is 'to search for' a lost or hidden thing. For house-hunting at an office, Koreans say 보러 왔어요 (to view) or 집 구하러 왔어요 (to secure a place), not 찾으러 왔어요.

english: Is it monthly rent or jeonse?
usage: Is it monthly rent or jeonse?
Polite; asking which rental scheme a listing is
반말, comparing options with a friend
Would this be monthly or jeonse?
반전세 = big deposit + smaller monthly, the in-between type
examples: 이 집 월세예요, 전세예요?
Is this place monthly rent or jeonse?
Pointing at one listing to pin down the scheme
전세는 부담돼서요, 월세로 보고 있어요.
Jeonse is too much for me, so I'm looking at monthly.
부담되다 ('to be a burden') explains why you want 월세
보증금 천에 월 오십이면 반전세네요?
10 million deposit and 500k a month — that's semi-jeonse, right?
Naming the deposit/monthly split to confirm it's 반전세
nuance: 월세 (月貰, 'monthly rent') and 전세 (傳貰, 'jeonse') are the two pillars of Korean renting, and you'll say this line constantly. 월세 means you pay a deposit (보증금) plus rent every month, like renting in most countries. 전세 is uniquely Korean: you hand the landlord one enormous lump sum (often 50–80% of the home's value) for the whole lease, pay ZERO monthly rent, and get the entire sum back when you move out — the landlord profits by investing your money. There's also 반전세 ('half-jeonse'): a large-ish deposit AND a smaller monthly rent, the middle ground. The dividing line learners blur is 보증금 vs. 전세금: in 월세 the deposit is a smallish security 보증금; in 전세 the lump sum IS the rent mechanism (전세금/전셋돈), not a 'deposit' in the Western sense. The English-speaker trap is calling 전세 a 'deposit' and expecting to also pay monthly — with true 전세 there is no monthly rent at all. Another trap is the particle/copula: it's 월세'예'요 after a vowel but you'll hear learners say 월세'이'에요 — the contracted 예요 is natural here. Always 존댓말 with an agent.

mistakes: Thinking 전세 means 'deposit' on top of monthly rent.
With 전세 you pay a huge lump sum and NO monthly rent, getting it all back at move-out. If there's monthly rent plus a deposit, that's 월세 (or 반전세), not 전세.
Confusing 보증금 with 전세금.
보증금 is the (usually smaller) security deposit in a 월세 contract; 전세금 is the whole lease sum in 전세. They aren't the same number or the same idea — ask 보증금 얼마예요? for 월세, 전세금 얼마예요? for 전세.
Saying 월세이에요 instead of 월세예요.
After the vowel-ending 월세, the copula contracts to 예요: 월세예요, 전세예요. 월세이에요 is the uncontracted, unnatural form.

usage: Polite; the first money question on any 월세 listing
반말, with a friend comparing places
Softer, 'how does the deposit work out?' — very natural to agents
Negotiating: trade a lower 보증금 for higher 월세
examples: 여기 보증금 얼마예요?
How much is the deposit here?
Asked while looking at a specific unit
보증금이 어떻게 돼요? 천에 오십이요? — 네, 맞아요.
What's the deposit — 10 million, 500k a month? — Yes, that's right.
천/오십 in 만원 units is the everyday way to say amounts
보증금을 조금 올리면 월세 좀 깎아 주실 수 있어요?
If I raise the deposit a bit, could you lower the monthly rent?
The classic 보증금↑ → 월세↓ trade, asked politely with 깎다
nuance: 보증금 (保證金, 'security deposit') is the up-front money the landlord holds against unpaid rent or damage, returned when you leave. In Korean renting, 보증금 and 월세 trade off on a sliding scale: a higher deposit usually buys a lower monthly rent and vice versa, so asking 보증금 얼마예요? is really asking where this unit sits on that scale. Amounts are spoken in 만원 (10,000-won) units, so '천' means 천만 원 (10 million) and '오십' means 오십만 원 (500k) — you almost never say the full digits. The very natural agent-friendly variant is 보증금이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does the deposit come out?'), softer than the bare 얼마예요?. The dividing line from 전세금 (the whole 전세 lump) is which contract you're in — don't ask 전세금 얼마예요? about a 월세 place. The English-speaker trap is the particle: with 얼마예요? you say 보증금 얼마예요? (no 이/가 needed in casual speech), but with 어떻게 돼요? you add 이: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요?. Another trap is treating 보증금 like a Western 'first-and-last month' — it's a single lump tied to the rent scheme, and it can be large (often 10–20× the monthly rent). Stay in 존댓말; this is a money negotiation with a professional.

Treating 보증금 like Western first-and-last-month rent.
보증금 is one lump tied to the rent scheme, often many times the monthly rent, and it slides against 월세. It is not 'two months' rent up front'; ask the actual figure and the trade-off.

usage: Polite; checking what's on top of rent
The flip side: asking if it's already baked in
What does the maintenance fee cover?
Drilling into what the 관리비 includes (water? internet?)
examples: 월세 말고 관리비는 따로예요?
Apart from rent, is there a separate maintenance fee?
월세 말고 ('aside from rent') frames the extra cost
관리비 얼마예요? 거기에 수도세 포함이에요?
How much is the maintenance fee? Is water included in it?
Ask the amount, then what 수도세 (water) it covers
관리비에 인터넷이랑 청소 포함이면 괜찮네요.
If internet and cleaning are in the maintenance fee, that's not bad.
Weighing the 관리비 by what's bundled (인터넷, 청소)
nuance: 관리비 (管理費, 'maintenance/management fee') is the monthly building charge ON TOP of your rent — covering things like cleaning of common areas, the elevator, security, hallway lighting, sometimes water (수도세), internet, or even heating, depending on the building. It can be a few 만원 in a small 원룸 or much more in an apartment complex, so 관리비는 따로예요? ('is it separate?') is an essential cost question. The dividing line is 따로 ('separate, on top') vs. 포함 (包含, 'included'): 관리비는 따로예요? asks if it's an extra charge, while 관리비 포함이에요? asks if it's already in the rent — they expect opposite yes/no answers, so don't muddle them. Crucially, always follow up with 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? because a 'cheap' rent can hide a fat 관리비, and what it bundles varies wildly. The English-speaker trap is assuming 관리비 is like a Western 'HOA fee' for owners only — no, renters pay it monthly too. Another trap is the topic particle: 관리비는 따로예요? uses 는 to set up the contrast ('as for the maintenance fee…'); dropping it is okay casually but the 는 sounds natural here. Use 존댓말 with the agent.

usage: Polite; asking what comes with the place
풀옵션 = fridge, washer, AC, bed, etc. all included
Asking about one specific 옵션 item
examples: 여기 옵션은 뭐가 있어요?
What's included here?
General check of what appliances/furniture come with the unit
풀옵션이에요? 세탁기랑 냉장고 다 있어요?
Is it full-option? Are the washer and fridge both there?
풀옵션 then confirm specific items 세탁기/냉장고
옵션에 침대는 없고 에어컨이랑 인덕션만 있어요.
No bed in the options, just AC and an induction stove.
Listing what IS and ISN'T included, item by item

This matters enormously because furnishing a Korean apartment yourself is costly, so 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? is one of the most practical viewing questions. The dividing line from 관리비 is category: 옵션 is the stuff INSIDE the unit, 관리비 is the monthly building charge — don't conflate 'what's included' across the two. The English-speaker trap is using 옵션 in its general English sense ('choices/alternatives') and confusing the agent — in housing it specifically means built-in appliances/furniture. Another trap is the particle: 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? sets 옵션 as the topic with 은, then asks 뭐가 있어요 ('what exists') — note it's 뭐'가' (subject) inside, a spot where learners wrongly say 뭐를. Confirm item by item, because '풀옵션' can still be missing the one thing you need (e.g. no 침대). Stay in 존댓말.

usage: Polite; asking the available move-in date
반말, casual 들어가다 ('go in') for moving in
More formal, naming 입주 가능일 ('available date')
Can I move in right away?
Asking if immediate move-in (즉시입주) is possible
examples: 이 집 언제 입주 가능해요?
When can I move into this place?
Pinning down availability on a unit you like
다음 달 초에 입주하고 싶은데 가능해요?
I'd like to move in early next month — is that possible?
State your target with 입주하고 싶다, then ask 가능해요
지금 사람이 살고 있어서 다음 달에나 입주 가능해요.
Someone's living here now, so move-in's only possible next month.
다음 달에나 ('not until next month') explains the wait
nuance: 입주 (入住, 'moving in / taking up residence') is the formal word for occupying a home, and 입주 가능해요? asks when the unit is free for you to move in. This is critical timing in Korea because leases, deposits, and the previous tenant's move-out all have to line up, and a place you love might not be 입주 가능 until weeks later. 즉시입주 ('immediate move-in') is a common listing tag; 바로 입주 돼요? asks for that. The dividing line from the casual 들어가다 ('to go in', also used for moving in) is register: 입주하다 is the proper real-estate verb on contracts and with agents, while 언제 들어갈 수 있어요? is the everyday spoken version — both fine, but 입주 sounds more 'official.' The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'move in' as 움직이다 ('to move/budge physically') or 이사 오다 in the wrong frame — 이사하다/이사 오다 is 'to relocate (the whole act)', while 입주 is specifically taking up the new residence; for the date a place becomes available, say 입주 가능해요?. Another trap is 가능하다's conjugation: it's 가능해요 (가능 + 하다), and learners sometimes say 가능있어요, which is wrong. Use 존댓말 with the agent.

usage: Polite; asking about natural light / direction

english: Could you lower the rent a bit?
usage: Please lower the rent a bit
반말, only with a friend, never the landlord

Couldn't you take just a little off the rent?
Softer, more pleading 'wouldn't it be okay if…'
At least waive some of the maintenance fee
Fallback: ask to cut 관리비 if rent won't budge
examples: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요. 오만 원만요.
Please lower the rent a bit — just 50,000 off.
Name a concrete cut (오만 원) to make the ask real
계약 바로 할 테니까 월세 좀 깎아 주시면 안 돼요?
I'll sign right away, so couldn't you lower the rent a little?
Offer to commit (계약 바로) as leverage to negotiate
보증금 더 낼 테니까 월세 좀 깎아 주세요.
I'll pay more deposit, so please lower the monthly rent.

hangul: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요?

usage: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요?
Can I look around a bit more?
Polite; asking for more time to inspect the unit
Can I look a bit more?
반말, with a friend who came along
Could I take my time looking?
Softer, asks to view at your own pace
Please show me other places too
Asking to see additional units beyond this one
examples: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? 화장실도 보고 싶어서요.
Can I look around a bit more? I'd like to see the bathroom too.
Give a reason (화장실도 보고 싶다) to extend the viewing
수압이랑 옵션 좀 천천히 볼 수 있을까요?
Could I take my time checking the water pressure and appliances?

이 집은 좀 그렇고, 다른 집도 보여 주세요.
This one's not quite it — please show me others too.
좀 그렇다 ('a bit meh') politely declines, then asks for more
nuance: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is 여기 ('here') + 좀 ('a bit', softener) + 더 ('more') + 볼 수 있어요 ('can I see?'), asking the agent for more time to inspect a unit — open closets, check the bathroom, test 수압 ('water pressure'), look for 곰팡이 ('mold'). Korean viewings can feel rushed because agents juggle many clients, so this phrase buys you the time to look properly. The dividing line from 다른 집도 보여 주세요 ('show me other places') is scope: 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? extends THIS viewing, while 보여 주세요 requests ADDITIONAL units — use the right one. Note 보다 ('to see/inspect') vs. 보여 주다 ('to show'): you 보다 the place yourself, the agent 보여 준다 (shows) it to you, so don't say 여기 좀 더 보여 줄 수 있어요? when you just want to keep looking on your own. ('may I look?') as if you need permission for everything; 볼 수 있어요? ('can I look more?') is softer and assumes cooperation. I'd like to take this place
Softer, stating preference before fully committing

I like it here. I'll take this place.
마음에 들다 ('to like/be pleased with') then decide
고민해 봤는데 그냥 이 집으로 할게요.
I thought it over and I'll just go with this place.
고민해 봤다 ('thought it over') shows you weighed it
이 집으로 할게요. 계약은 언제 할 수 있어요?

nuance: 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요? is 집주인 ('house owner/landlord') + 이랑 ('with') + 직접 ('directly/in person') + 얘기하다 ('to talk') + ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can I?'), asking to deal with the actual owner rather than only the agent — important for clarifying repairs, rules, and whether the person signing is truly the owner (a fraud safeguard). 집주인 is the everyday word; the honorific is 집주인분 / 임대인 (賃貸人, the formal 'lessor' on contracts), versus you the 임차인 (賃借人, 'lessee'). The dividing line from the agent is role: the 부동산 (agent/공인중개사, licensed broker) brokers the deal and earns a 복비/중개수수료 (brokerage fee), while the 집주인 owns the place — for binding promises (repairs, move-in date), you want the owner's word. The English-speaker trap is the particle 이랑 vs. 하고/와: all mean 'with', but 이랑 is the casual-natural choice in speech (집주인이랑); 와/과 is more formal/written. Another trap is 직역-ing 'directly' as 똑바로 ('straight/upright') — 직접 ('in person, firsthand') is the right word for dealing with someone directly; 똑바로 means physically straight. Also verify the signer is the registered owner on the 등기부등본 — a key anti-fraud step. Use 존댓말, and refer to the owner with honorifics (집주인분, -세요) even when they're not present.

nuance: 복비는 얼마예요? is 복비 (the colloquial word for the real-estate agent's commission, a contraction of 복덕방 비(費) — 복덕방(福德房) being the old-fashioned word for a realtor's office) + 은 (topic) + 얼마예요? ('how much?'). The formal term is 중개수수료 (仲介手數料, 'brokerage fee') or 중개보수, and rates are legally capped on a sliding 요율표 (rate table) based on the deposit/rent and property type — so the fee isn't arbitrary, and you can ask the agent to show the rate. Crucially, BOTH the landlord and the tenant each pay their own 복비 to the agent (각자 부담), a fact that surprises newcomers expecting only one side to pay. The dividing line from 보증금/월세 is who gets the money: 복비 goes to the 부동산 (agent), not the landlord, and it's a ONE-time cost at contract, not monthly. The English-speaker trap is not budgeting for it at all (treating the agent as 'free' like a listing site) and then being startled at signing. Another trap is register: 복비 is fine in speech, but on receipts and formally it's 중개수수료 — recognize both. Also ask 현금영수증 돼요? ('can I get a cash receipt?') for your records, and confirm the agent is a licensed 공인중개사 (certified broker) — unlicensed brokering is a fraud red flag. The fee is negotiable only within the legal cap. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent.
